---
name: concept-space-additions-map
description: Adding new rule families to arbitrary_exception_rule_prior barely moves MAP ll (~-1067); which additions were tried
metadata:
  type: project
---
Round 3 (2026-10-30), adding one new rule family (own Dirichlet weight) to the incumbent arbitrary_exception_rule_prior (MAP ll -1067.0):
- offset residue classes r mod k, k=3..6: -1066.7 (best; submitted as offset_progression_concepts, iter_3/candidate_0)
- same with k up to 12 or 25: -1067.2, weight -> 0
- multiples of 13..50: -1067.8; digit-sum = s: -1067.2 (weight 0.08); odd multiples/2-adic: -1067.2; decade blocks: -1067.3
After 69,9,39,21 the model still predicts 0.61 "yes" for 19 (observed 0/5), even with offset progressions in the space.
**Why:** the concept space is not the bottleneck. Remaining residuals are scattered single cells with n=5.
**How to apply:** don't spend another round on concept-space additions. See [[powers-of-2-37-misfit]].

Round 4 (2026-10-30), iter_4/candidate_1: a rule-vs-range prior log-odds that grows linearly with the number of examples (rule_noticing_grows_with_examples), added to parity_within_range_concepts. MAP ll -1063.98 for both models; the slope ≈ 0.03. The set size does not change how readily people think of a rule, so don't retry this.
---
name: experiment2-iter1-critique-stats
description: exp2 iter_1 critique of beta_share_width_exception_concepts — the 8 PPC stats chosen and observed values, so later rounds avoid repeats
metadata:
  type: project
---
iter_1 critique (2026-10-30) stats, with observed values: wide_spread_inrange_yes_rate 0.53 (>=3 ex, span>=60); within_cell_disagreement 0.34; set_size_inrange_contrast (2-ex minus 4-ex inside range) -0.11; sparse_rule_numeric_neighbor_yes 0.00 (50 trials, all no); sparse_rule_member_yes 0.61; last_digit_vs_parity_contrast 0.76; below_minus_above_outside_yes -0.06; interior_proximity_gradient -0.03.

**Why:** iter_0's 8 stats were all null ([[prior-leaking-judgment]]); this records what iter_1 probed.
**How to apply:** check iter_1/critique/ppc_results.json for which came out significant before choosing new stats; see [[experiment2-data-structure]].
---
name: experiment2-data-structure
description: experiment2 responses = 10 participants x 450 trials, 2 stimulus orders; PPC keeps row order; shown-example targets get only 62% yes
metadata:
  type: project
---
experiment2 (2026-10-30): responses.csv is 4500 rows = 10 participants × 450 (participant = cumsum(trial_index==0)), only 2 distinct stimulus sequences; 119 sets. The PPC harness (src/critique/ppc.py) copies the CSV and overwrites only `rating`, so row-order/participant/lag statistics are valid.
Raw observations: when the target is one of the shown examples (85 trials) the yes rate is only 0.62 — the lapse-free incumbent predicts ~1, so a lapse/guessing term looks likely to be needed. Session late-minus-early yes rate -0.06; participant yes-rate SD 0.087.
**Why:** iter_0 critique statistics were built on this structure.
**How to apply:** check the iter_0 ppc_results.json for which of these turned out significant; see [[round4-null-refinements]] for the experiment1 data layout.

"""Refinement of gamma_width_exception_family_concepts: the same Bayesian concept
learning over 45 rules (family-organised prior, exception rules as their own
family) and all intervals of 1..100, with the size principle (examples come from
the concept with probability 0.9). The single change is the form of the prior
over a range's width: instead of a gamma over the width (unbounded, so ranges
spanning nearly all of 1..100 keep a sizeable prior), people hold a beta prior
over the share of the 1..100 line a range covers, with mean share and
concentration inferred. A range is a part of the number line, so very wide
ranges ("any number") are as implausible as very narrow ones, and widely spread
examples are explained by a rule rather than by an almost-everything range.
"""

import numpy as np
import pymc as pm
import pytensor.tensor as pt
from scipy.special import logsumexp

ALPHA = 0.9
NUMBERS = np.arange(1, 101)


def rule_concepts():
    rules = {
        "odd": [n for n in NUMBERS if n % 2 == 1],
        "primes": [n for n in NUMBERS if n > 1 and all(n % a for a in range(2, int(n**0.5) + 1))],
        "squares": [n * n for n in range(1, 11)],
        "cubes": [n**3 for n in range(1, 5)],
        "powers of 2, not 32": [2, 4, 8, 16, 64],
        "powers of 2, or 37": [2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 37, 64],
        "even": list(range(2, 101, 2)),
    }
    rules.update({f"multiples of {m}": list(range(m, 101, m)) for m in [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12]})
    rules.update({f"powers of {m}": [m**k for k in range(1, 8) if m**k <= 100] for m in range(2, 11)})
    rules.update({f"ends in {d}": [n for n in NUMBERS if n % 10 == d] for d in range(10)})
    rules.update({f"contains digit {d}": [n for n in NUMBERS if str(d) in str(n)] for d in range(10)})
    return rules


_RULES = rule_concepts()
RULE_NAMES, RULES = list(_RULES), list(_RULES.values())
N_RULES = len(RULES)
INTERVALS = [list(range(m, n + 1)) for m in NUMBERS for n in range(m, 101)]
MEMBERSHIP = np.array([np.isin(NUMBERS, c) for c in RULES + INTERVALS], dtype="float64")
EXAMPLE_LOG_LIK = np.log(ALPHA * MEMBERSHIP / MEMBERSHIP.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True) + (1 - ALPHA) / 100)
RULE_MEMBERSHIP = MEMBERSHIP[:N_RULES]
INTERVAL_MEMBERSHIP = MEMBERSHIP[N_RULES:]
INTERVAL_SIZE_IDX = (INTERVAL_MEMBERSHIP.sum(axis=1) - 1).astype("int64")  # L - 1
SIZES = np.arange(1, 101, dtype="float64")
LOG_N_OF_SIZE = np.log(101.0 - SIZES)  # number of intervals of each size
SHARE = (SIZES - 0.5) / 100.0  # share of the 1..100 line covered, in (0, 1)

def rule_family(name):
    if name in ("odd", "even"):
        return 0
    if name == "primes":
        return 1
    if name in ("squares", "cubes"):
        return 2
    if name.startswith("powers of 2,"):
        return 7
    if name.startswith("powers"):
        return 3
    if name.startswith("multiples"):
        return 4
    if name.startswith("ends in"):
        return 5
    return 6


FAMILY = np.array([rule_family(n) for n in RULE_NAMES])
N_FAMILIES = FAMILY.max() + 1
FAMILY_SIZE = np.bincount(FAMILY)

# All intervals of one size share their prior, so prepare_observed sums each
# set's interval likelihood within every size (parameter-free) and records, per
# size, the share of that evidence from intervals containing each target.

with pm.Model() as model:
    rule_log_lik = pm.Data("rule_log_lik", np.zeros((1, N_RULES)))  # (sets, rules)
    size_log_evidence = pm.Data("size_log_evidence", np.zeros((1, 100)))  # (sets, sizes): log sum_j P(D|j)
    cell_set = pm.Data("cell_set", np.zeros(1, dtype="int64"))  # (cells,)
    cell_rule_member = pm.Data("cell_rule_member", np.zeros((1, N_RULES)))  # (cells, rules)
    cell_size_member = pm.Data("cell_size_member", np.zeros((1, 100)))  # (cells, sizes)
    row_cell = pm.Data("row_cell", np.zeros(1, dtype="int64"))  # (trials,)
    rating = pm.Data("rating", np.zeros(1, dtype="int64"))

    lambda_0 = pm.Beta("lambda_0", 2, 2)
    mean_share = pm.Beta("mean_share", 2, 3)  # mean share of 1..100 a range covers
    concentration = pm.LogNormal("concentration", mu=np.log(5.0), sigma=1.0)
    family_weights = pm.Dirichlet("family_weights", a=np.full(N_FAMILIES, 2.0))
    rule_log_prior = pt.log(family_weights)[FAMILY] - np.log(FAMILY_SIZE[FAMILY])

    log_size_prior = ((mean_share * concentration - 1.0) * np.log(SHARE)
                      + ((1.0 - mean_share) * concentration - 1.0) * np.log1p(-SHARE))
    log_size_prior = log_size_prior - pt.logsumexp(log_size_prior)
    log_per_interval = log_size_prior - LOG_N_OF_SIZE  # prior of one interval of size L

    log_rules = pt.log(lambda_0) + rule_log_prior[None, :] + rule_log_lik
    log_sizes = pt.log1p(-lambda_0) + log_per_interval[None, :] + size_log_evidence
    log_joint = pt.concatenate([log_rules, log_sizes], axis=1)
    posterior = pt.exp(log_joint - pt.logsumexp(log_joint, axis=1, keepdims=True))
    cell_post = posterior[cell_set]
    in_concept = ((cell_post[:, :N_RULES] * cell_rule_member).sum(axis=1)
                  + (cell_post[:, N_RULES:] * cell_size_member).sum(axis=1))

    p_yes = pm.Deterministic("p_yes", pt.clip(in_concept[row_cell], 1e-6, 1 - 1e-6))
    pm.Bernoulli("response", p=p_yes, observed=rating)


def prepare_observed(rows):
    """Rows carry `number_set` ("16,8", in presented order), `target` and `rating`."""
    sets = [tuple(int(x) for x in str(r["number_set"]).split(",")) for r in rows]
    unique = list(dict.fromkeys(sets))
    index = {s: i for i, s in enumerate(unique)}
    set_log_lik = np.stack([EXAMPLE_LOG_LIK[:, np.array(s) - 1].sum(axis=1) for s in unique])
    n_sets = len(unique)
    size_ev = np.zeros((n_sets, 100))
    size_member = np.zeros((n_sets, 100, 100))
    for i in range(n_sets):
        ll = set_log_lik[i, N_RULES:]
        for L in range(100):
            sel = INTERVAL_SIZE_IDX == L
            ev = logsumexp(ll[sel])
            size_ev[i, L] = ev
            size_member[i, L] = np.exp(ll[sel] - ev) @ INTERVAL_MEMBERSHIP[sel]
    keys = [(index[s], int(r["target"])) for s, r in zip(sets, rows)]
    cells = list(dict.fromkeys(keys))
    cell_index = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(cells)}
    cell_s = np.array([c[0] for c in cells], dtype="int64")
    cell_t = np.array([c[1] - 1 for c in cells], dtype="int64")
    return {
        "rule_log_lik": set_log_lik[:, :N_RULES],
        "size_log_evidence": size_ev,
        "cell_set": cell_s,
        "cell_rule_member": RULE_MEMBERSHIP[:, cell_t].T.copy(),
        "cell_size_member": np.clip(size_member[cell_s, :, cell_t], 0.0, 1.0),
        "row_cell": np.array([cell_index[k] for k in keys], dtype="int64"),
        "rating": np.array([int(r["rating"]) for r in rows], dtype="int64"),
    }

content.text:
I've written all three files for the new model, `off_by_one_power_concepts`, and it passes the check command (`OK`). That check skips novelty against the other models, and with only one chain it couldn't measure convergence (R-hat). Admission's full fit will decide both.

**Hypothesis:** people learn the concept the same way as the current best model, `beta_share_width_exception_concepts`. The one difference is that they also consider "near-misses" of the sparse multiplicative rules: numbers one more or one less than a square, a cube, or a power of 2 to 10. Examples are 1, 3, 7, 15, 31, 63 and 3, 5, 9, 17, 33, 65. These near-miss rules are their own kind of rule, and the data set how plausible people find them. So after 31, 3, 1, 15 people should say yes to 63 but not to other odd numbers.

**Why this one:** the critique found no significant gaps in the best model, so I picked the addition from the stimuli. Several example sets in experiment 2 are exactly such shifted powers (31,3,1; 31,3,1,15; 33,17,5,9; 33,3,65; 7,63; 3,7).

**Implementation:** `candidate.py` is a copy of the best model plus a ninth rule family with its own prior weight. It holds 10 distinct near-miss rules (duplicates and rules with fewer than 3 members are dropped), for 55 rules in total. No other part of the model changed. The smoke fit took 13 seconds, with a log-likelihood of −2270.0.

**Expect a small effect at most:**
- Few targets actually test these sets. After 31, 3, 1, 15, only 2 of 5 answers to 63 were yes.
- Adding new rule families before (in experiment 1) gained almost nothing.
- The model may also be rejected as a near-duplicate of the best model, if the two make nearly the same predictions on the novelty test stimuli.

I saved a memory note on this candidate so later rounds can check whether the near-miss rules got any prior weight.

Files are in `_runs/cell_1/experiment2/model_loop/iter_1/candidate_2/`:
- `hypothesis.md`
- `model_name.txt`
- `candidate.py`
